title: Things to do in Ravenna: 5 places for mosaics and history
description: Explore five Ravenna places: San Vitale, Galla Placidia, Sant’Apollinare Nuovo, Dante’s Tomb and Piazza del Popolo, with ticket choices and a practical route.
intro: For a first visit to Ravenna, this selection brings together the Basilica of San Vitale, the Mausoleum of Galla Placidia, Sant’Apollinare Nuovo, Dante’s Tomb and Piazza del Popolo. These five places in the historic centre combine mosaics, literary memory and the civic life of the city. The most useful decision comes before the walk: choose an appropriate admission itinerary and book Galla Placidia’s entry slot. The five places in this guide are a different selection from the operator’s ticket called the five-monument itinerary.

Ravenna lies in Emilia-Romagna, near the Adriatic coast. Its UNESCO-listed Early Christian property comprises eight specific monuments from the fifth and sixth centuries; that designation does not cover every central building or every stop below. San Vitale, Galla Placidia and Sant’Apollinare Nuovo belong to the group. Dante’s Tomb and the square bring different periods into the picture. Arrange interiors around actual reservations and leave space for walking, meals and observation: a line on a map cannot establish opening arrangements or the right pace for your group.

quickFacts.label: Location
quickFacts.value: Ravenna, Emilia-Romagna, north-eastern Italy, near the Adriatic.

quickFacts.label: Focus
quickFacts.value: Three mosaic monuments, Dante’s Tomb and the main civic square.

quickFacts.label: Key reservation
quickFacts.value: Galla Placidia requires a booked entry time and a ticket that includes it.

quickFacts.label: Route
quickFacts.value: A historic-centre walk adapted to admission slots, breaks and mobility needs.

sections.heading: 1. Basilica of San Vitale: reading power in the mosaics
paragraphs: Give San Vitale an interior visit with time for the presbytery and apse. Consecrated in 547, the basilica combines Western and Eastern artistic traditions that help explain Byzantine Ravenna. The panels of Justinian and Theodora provide a useful starting point: identify the rulers, their attendants and the offerings they hold. Consider how authority is represented alongside the religious setting. These are not souvenirs of an imperial visit; the operator explicitly points out that neither ruler ever visited Ravenna.

Then look at Christ seated on the celestial globe and Bishop Ecclesius presenting the model of the church. Following these relationships between figures, objects and architecture offers more than trying to photograph every surface without understanding the overall arrangement. San Vitale stands near Via Cavour in the historic centre and forms one visiting cluster with Galla Placidia. Grouping them avoids crossing the city twice, but being next to one another does not give them identical admission conditions.

Ravenna Mosaici’s smallest published itinerary includes San Vitale and Sant’Apollinare Nuovo. To add Galla Placidia, check another ticket option and the required timed reservation. Read the calendar for your particular date, especially around public holidays. The operator distinguishes summer and winter periods and asks for silence and appropriate clothing: this remains a church as well as a heritage monument. If you need an adapted entrance, check the actual route described for visitors with reduced mobility before travelling.

sections.heading: 2. Mausoleum of Galla Placidia: prepare for a short interior visit
paragraphs: The contrast between the brick exterior and decorated interior makes Galla Placidia a rewarding companion to San Vitale. The small Latin-cross building stands just behind the basilica. Inside, look for the star-filled dome and its golden cross, then the image of Christ as the Good Shepherd over the entrance. The transition from outdoor light to the dim interior is a reason to let your eyes settle before moving between scenes. The archive photograph helps identify the building; it does not establish present-day access or availability.

The familiar name can suggest the wrong story: Galla Placidia is not buried here. The municipal account explains that she died in Rome in 450 and was buried there, so this building never fulfilled its intended funerary role for her. That distinction shifts the visit away from searching for an imperial tomb. The interest lies in the connection between the small architecture, Christian imagery and the decoration filling the upper parts of the interior.

Book an entry time and make sure the ticket you purchase includes this monument. The operator publishes a five-minute visit and limits longer stays during busy periods to protect the interior microclimate. Arrive with an idea of what you want to notice, and follow your slot and the staff’s instructions. Do not plan an extended photo session or rely on rushing every later stop to recover from a missed reservation. A break before or after this cluster is more comfortable than organizing the day as a chain of tightly spaced entrances.

sections.heading: 3. Sant’Apollinare Nuovo: finding the layers of history
paragraphs: Sant’Apollinare Nuovo is on Via di Roma in the historic centre. When buying tickets or following directions, distinguish it from Sant’Apollinare in Classe, a separate basilica. Nuovo was built as Theodoric’s palace church and changed from Arian worship to Catholic orthodoxy in the sixth century. Its mosaics reveal that the surviving decoration does not belong to one unchanging moment: images were altered as political authority and religious use changed.

Divide your attention between the upper scenes from Christ’s life and the lower band showing Classis, the palace and the processions of male and female saints. In the palace representation, hands left behind after figures were removed make a later alteration visible. You do not need to learn the entire iconographic programme to appreciate the place. Choosing one group of images and following its arrangement is a practical way to look carefully instead of treating the interior as a quick photographic stop.

The operator’s suggested route for train arrivals begins here and continues on foot through the centre. That can work well if it fits your Galla Placidia reservation; reverse the order if the booked slot comes first. Keep your ticket ready to show at each monument. Inclusion in a combined itinerary does not mean unlimited re-entry: check validity and the number of admissions. The operator lists access at Nuovo for visitors with reduced mobility, while individual requirements should be confirmed before the journey.

sections.heading: 4. Dante’s Tomb: understanding the Zone of Silence
paragraphs: Dante’s Tomb stands at Via Dante Alighieri 9 in the area called the Zone of Silence. Camillo Morigia’s small Neoclassical temple changes the focus of the walk: this is a place of literary memory rather than another mosaic cycle. The inscription above the entrance identifies the monument. Inside are the poet’s sepulchre and Pietro Lombardo’s relief. The municipal account also describes the votive lamp burning oil donated by Tuscany, a material connection between the city holding Dante’s remains and his native region.

Treat this as a view from outside. The official listing states free admission but explains that the tomb can only be viewed from the exterior, with a physical-disability access limitation. That is different from a room open for visitors to walk around. Respect the character of the area, keep the approach clear and check hours and closures for your date. The stop fits naturally into the central walk without adding a diocesan ticket reservation. Conditions here should not be confused with those of nearby museums, which have their own admissions and visits.

sections.heading: 5. Piazza del Popolo: the civic city between monument visits
paragraphs: Piazza del Popolo introduces civic Ravenna between visits to religious heritage. Several central streets converge on this square, framed by buildings of municipal government and the prefecture. Identify Palazzo Merlato, the town hall, and look at the two columns with Saints Apollinaris and Vitalis. Their presence connects Venetian rule with later changes to the city’s public symbols. Read the square as a relationship between façades, entrances and public space rather than a checklist of institutional interiors to enter.

Use it as an orientation point and a flexible interval between reservations. Checking your next direction or pausing here makes more sense than using Galla Placidia’s short slot for those tasks. The municipal listing describes the square as accessible to visitors with physical disabilities, although that does not automatically establish the accessibility of every approach, crossing or nearby service. It is a public space without an admission from the mosaic itinerary. The surrounding institutional buildings retain their own functions; viewing a façade does not imply that its interior is open for sightseeing.

sections.heading: Choosing tickets: two different lists of five
paragraphs: This guide selects five places, while Ravenna Mosaici sells itineraries for two, four or five diocesan monuments. The two-monument option combines San Vitale and Sant’Apollinare Nuovo. The four-monument option adds Galla Placidia and the Neonian Baptistery; the five-monument option also includes the Archiepiscopal Museum and Saint Andrew’s Chapel. Dante’s Tomb and Piazza del Popolo do not belong to that ticket. To visit our three interiors, find a product including Galla and compare the other admissions it provides, even if you decide not to use every one.

Official information describes seven-day validity and one admission per monument, but always review the terms for the product and date you choose before paying. Galla requires a booked time; the wider product brings other mandatory slots. Save or print the electronic ticket to show at every entrance. The published calendar distinguishes seasons and lists Christmas and New Year’s Day closures, so holidays should not be assumed to follow ordinary arrangements. No single price is quoted here: the appropriate itinerary, eligible concessions and actual availability are more relevant to the purchase.

sections.heading: Arriving by train and adapting the walk
paragraphs: Ravenna station has its main entrance at Piazzale Farini and another on Via Antico Squero towards the Darsena. It stands beside the central limited-traffic area. For a journey from Bologna or another Italian stop, check the actual railway service, changes, arrival time and return. Cities being relatively close does not establish a direct train at any hour. If you are continuing through Italy, the Bologna, Ferrara and Venice guides offer separate sightseeing plans, each requiring its own transport rather than becoming automatic additions to this day.

The centre has a broad pedestrian area. For bus connections, the municipal reference is Start Romagna and its current route information. If driving, select parking and check the ZTL before approaching your accommodation: motor traffic is restricted and electronically monitored. For reduced mobility, examine each monument and connection rather than relying on map distances. The operator describes adapted routes at San Vitale and Galla and access at Nuovo; Dante’s warning is different. On wet days, leave more room for the walks between buildings and use the booked admissions as the fixed points in your plan.

itinerary: Arrival and Via di Roma block: if your Galla slot allows it, start at Sant’Apollinare Nuovo after arriving at the station. Give its interior time for the different mosaic bands rather than treating it as a place to pass through. Continue towards Dante’s area and make the exterior stop with respect for the Zone of Silence. This sequence is a planning suggestion, not a guarantee of openings or the time required by every visitor.

Civic-centre block: pass through Piazza del Popolo to observe the town hall, columns and the square’s relationship with the central streets. Include food and rest at your own pace while keeping a comfortable margin before the reserved entry. If walking is not practical for a connection, resolve the stops and access arrangements beforehand; improvising a vehicle directly to a monument can conflict with central traffic restrictions.

San Vitale and Galla Placidia block: group these monuments together and use Galla’s booked time as the anchor. Place San Vitale before or afterwards according to available time and current hours. With a longer stay, spread interiors across days within your ticket conditions. During a short visit, reduce the number of interiors before accumulating closely spaced reservations. Seeing these five places does not require five separate admission purchases.

faq.question: What should I see on a first visit to Ravenna?
faq.answer: This selection combines San Vitale, Galla Placidia, Sant’Apollinare Nuovo, Dante’s Tomb and Piazza del Popolo. The first three belong to the UNESCO mosaic-monument group; the other two add literary and civic history. Galla’s reservation and your dates’ opening arrangements help determine the order of the walk.

faq.question: Does the five-monument ticket cover the five places in this guide?
faq.answer: They are different lists. The diocesan five-monument itinerary contains San Vitale, Nuovo, Galla Placidia, the Neonian Baptistery and the Archiepiscopal Museum with Saint Andrew’s Chapel. Dante’s Tomb and Piazza del Popolo are outside that ticket. Choose the product covering the interiors you want and check its mandatory reservations.

faq.question: Do I need to reserve Galla Placidia?
faq.answer: Yes. The operator requires a booked entry time and a ticket that includes the mausoleum. It also publishes a short visiting period and restrictions on longer stays during busy times for conservation reasons. Arrive ready to follow the slot; do not assume that a general ticket without a specific time permits entry whenever you choose.

faq.question: Is Sant’Apollinare Nuovo the basilica at Classe?
faq.answer: No. Nuovo is on Via di Roma in the historic centre and is the church covered here. Sant’Apollinare in Classe is another monument in the UNESCO group. Verify the complete name before buying an itinerary or following directions, because confusing them changes both the transport and sightseeing plan.

faq.question: Can I follow this route without a car?
faq.answer: The station is beside the centre, and official sources describe walking connections between the monuments. This selection can be organized on foot when that suits your needs and reserved times. Check Start Romagna for other connections. Accessibility must be assessed place by place rather than inferred solely from distance.

conclusion: Ravenna becomes more rewarding when you connect its different stories: imperial authority at San Vitale, Galla Placidia’s symbolic imagery, the changes visible at Nuovo, and the literary and civic memories of the centre. Choose admissions for what they include, respect reserved times and allow space for the streets between monuments. The related Bologna, Ferrara and Venice guides can help you continue through Italy without compressing several cities into a hurried checklist.
